title: The Niggun: A Song Without Words
hookLine: the niggun climbs from sadness to joy to stillness
carry: a wordless niggun climbs toward god
tomorrow: The Rebbetzins and the Maiden of Ludmir
last: DRESS THAT REMEMBERS, DRESS TO MEET GOD.

cards: Yai, dai, bim, bam. What do those syllables mean? Nothing.
You won't find them in a dictionary. And yet a group of Hasidim can sing them over and over, slow at first, almost sad. Then the tune picks up.
Hands drum on whatever is nearby. Somebody stands. And then, somehow, it slows again, softer and softer, until the singers are only breathing.
The song leads them there. Hasidim have a name for that kind of song, and a picture for where it takes you.

teach.b: A ladder of song. The Hebrew word is niggun, a melody, and in Hasidic life it often means a tune sung without words. First, why no words.
Words can only say what they say. Hasidic teachers describe the wordless tune as reaching past language, to a place the heart knows but can't name. A syllable like yai has nothing to argue with.
Second, the climb. Some niggunim move in stages.
They begin in longing, sometimes close to sadness. They rise into joy. And some end in stillness, a quiet the song has earned.
That's the ladder: down where you are, up toward God, and then a rung where even the song stops. In Genesis, Jacob dreams of "a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven."
The niggun is a ladder you can sing. Third, an old precedent.

In the book of Kings, the prophet Elisha needs to hear God's word, and he asks for music first: "But now bring me a minstrel. And it came to pass, when the minstrel played, that the hand of the LORD came upon him."
Music came before the message. Fourth, how it lives. Courts keep their own niggunim, some said to come from their founding rebbes, and pass them down like the coats from yesterday.
Tradition says some Hasidic leaders composed tunes, and some adopted folk melodies they heard around them, believing a holy spark was waiting inside.
A shepherd's song could become a prayer.

how: Hasidim sing niggunim at the Shabbat table, at a rebbe's gathering, before prayer and at celebrations; a tune is often repeated many times, slowly building and then quieting.

games.q: you are Elisha. kings are waiting for a word from God. what do you ask for first?
games.why: "bring me a minstrel." when the minstrel played, the hand of the LORD came upon him. music came before the message.

practice: Hum a slow tune, any you know or just a few notes on one syllable like yai or dai, starting low and a little sad if that's where you are.

Let it lift on its own, brighter and faster if it wants to, then slow again, softer, until you're only humming on the breath. Stop, and stay in the quiet the tune left behind; if you can't make a sound where you are, hum it inside.
